items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (Acceleration due to gravity): A pinecone is dropped from rest from a tree. After 1.5 s, one student reports 𝑣= + 14.7 m/s and another reports

question.html: 𝑣= −14.7 m/s. Why must a coordinate system be defined, and can both be right?

body.html: The sign of 𝑎 (and of 𝑣) depends on which direction you call positive.
If down is positive, 𝑎= + 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> and 𝑣= + (9.8)(1.5) = + 14.7 m/s. If up is positive, 𝑎= −9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> and 𝑣= −14.7 m/s.

answer.html: Both can be right: they chose opposite positive directions. The sign of the acceleration, velocity, and displacement depends on the chosen positive direction, so you must define it first and use it consistently.

check.html: The speed (14.7 m/s) and the downward direction are the same either way.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (Rising and falling motion): A ball is thrown upward at 25 m/s. Its velocities at 1 s, 2 s, 3 s are +15.2, +5.4 and −4.4 m/s. During which second does it stop and reverse? How can you tell?

body.html: The velocity changes sign between 2 s and 3 s (exactly zero at 𝑡= 25 / 9.8 = 2.55 s).

answer.html: During the third second (between 𝑡= 2 s and 𝑡= 3 s), because that is when the velocity changes from positive to negative.

check.html: Matches the zero crossing at about 2.55 s.

items.title: Lesson 3, Analyze (Figure 21): A ball is thrown upward at 18.0 m/s. With up positive, its velocity-time graph is a straight line from +18.0 m/s at 0 to −18.0 m/s at 3.67 s. What would the graph look like if downward were chosen as the positive direction?

body.html: Flipping the positive direction flips the signs of 𝑣 and 𝑎.
The initial velocity becomes −18.0 m/s (upward), the acceleration is +9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>, and the velocity at 3.67 s is +18.0 m/s (downward). It crosses zero at 18.0 / 9.8 = 1.84 s.

answer.html: The graph would be the mirror image across the time axis: a straight line sloping upward from −18.0 m/s at 𝑡= 0 through zero at 1.84 s to +18.0 m/s at 3.67 s (slope +9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>).

check.html: Same physical motion, opposite sign convention.

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (Figure 22): A ball is dropped from rest from a bridge. With down positive and distance measured from the release point, what is the shape of its position- time graph?

answer.html: An upward-opening parabola that starts with zero slope at the release point and becomes steeper and steeper, because the velocity (the slope) increases steadily from zero. The shape shows how position changes with time, not the ball's path (which is a straight vertical line).

items.title: Lesson 3, Get It? (Acceleration at the top): A rock is thrown straight up on the Moon, where the free-fall acceleration is 1.62 m/s2. What are the rock's velocity and acceleration at the highest point?

answer.html: 𝑣= 0 and 𝑎= 1.62 m/s<sup>2</sup> downward.

check.html: The rock must start moving downward right after the peak.

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problem 45 (Challenge): A rubber ball is dropped from 2.0 m above the floor. After its first bounce it rises to 1.2 m, and after its second bounce to 0.60 m. Taking downward as positive, sketch the velocity-time and position-time graphs (position measured downward from the release point) from release until the ball lands after its second rise.

body.html: Release height 2.0 m, bounce heights 1.2 m and 0.60 m. In flight 𝑎= + 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> always.
Between bounces the ball is in free fall, so the 𝑣-𝑡 graph has slope +9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> and the 𝑥-𝑡 graph is made of parabolas. A bounce reverses the velocity almost instantly.

Speeds at the floor: before bounce 1, √2𝑔(2.0) = 6.3 m/s (down, + ); after, √2𝑔(1.2) = 4.8 m/s up (−4.8); before bounce 2, +4.8; after, √2𝑔(0.60) = 3.4 m/s up ( −3.4); before landing again, +3.4. Times: first fall 0.64 s, the first up-and-down 0.99 s, the second up-and-down 0.70 s. Position below the release point: the floor is at +2.0 m; the ball's highest points are at 0, 0.8 m, and 1.4 m below the release point.

answer.html: A set of parallel, upward-sloping straight line segments (slope +9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>): from 0 to +6.3 m/s, then a jump to −4.8 m/s and a rise through zero to +4.8 m/s, then a jump to −3.4 m/s and another rising segment to +3.4 m/s. Each bounce is a sudden vertical jump downward on the graph.

A series of parabolic arcs that meet at sharp corners (cusps) at the floor (𝑥= + 2.0 m ); the arcs get smaller with each bounce, with turning points 0.8 m and 1.4 m below the release point (heights 1.2 and 0.60 m above the floor). Distance is plotted downward.

check.html: A bounce reverses velocity in a very short time, so the 𝑣-𝑡 graph jumps and the 𝑥-𝑡 graph has a corner.

items.title: Lesson 3, Check Your Progress, Problem 46: A steel washer and a flat sheet of tissue paper are dropped from the same height. Which is closer to free fall? What can you do so the tissue also falls nearly as a free-falling object?

body.html: Free fall means gravity is the only significant force.

The washer is dense and compact; air resistance on it is tiny compared with its weight. The flat tissue feels a large air-resistance force compared with its small weight, so it drifts down slowly. Crumpling the tissue into a ball reduces the air resistance compared with its weight.

answer.html: The washer is nearly in free fall (air resistance negligible); the flat tissue is not. Crumpling the tissue into a tight ball makes it fall nearly with the washer.

check.html: In a vacuum both would fall together.

items.title: Lesson 3, Check Your Progress, Problem 49: A rock is thrown upward on the Moon, where 𝑔 is about one-sixth of Earth's. Compared with the same throw on Earth (same initial velocity), (a) how does the maximum height compare, and (b) how does the flight time compare?

body.html: Same 𝑣<sup>i</sup>; 𝑔<sub>Moon</sub> = 𝑔/ 6.

Maximum height ℎ= 𝑣<sub>i</sub> <sup>2</sup> / (2𝑔), flight time 𝑇= 2𝑣<sub>i</sub> / 𝑔. Both are inversely proportional to 𝑔. With 𝑔→𝑔/ 6 each is multiplied by 6. (Example: 𝑣<sub>i</sub> = 12 m/s gives 7.3 m and 2.4 s on Earth, and 44 m and 15 s on the Moon.)

answer.html: The maximum height is 6 times as great on the Moon.
The flight time is 6 times as long on the Moon.

items.title: Lesson 3, Check Your Progress, Problem 50: A stone is tossed straight up from a bridge at 12 m/s. Describe its velocity and acceleration while it rises, at the top, and while it falls (up positive).

body.html: Free-fall acceleration is constant and downward.

With up positive, 𝑣 starts at +12 m/s and decreases by 9.8 m/s every second: +2.2 m/s at 1.0 s, zero at 12 / 9.8 = 1.2 s, and −7.6 m/s at 2.0 s. The acceleration stays −9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> the whole time.

answer.html: The velocity decreases steadily: upward and slowing, zero at the top, then downward and speeding up. The acceleration does not change: it is 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> downward throughout.

check.html: A straight 𝑣-𝑡 line with constant negative slope.

items.title: Lesson 3, Check Your Progress, Problem 51 (Critical Thinking): A classmate says that at the very top of a basketball's flight "gravity stops acting for an instant, since the ball is not moving." Is the ball accelerating at its highest point? Devise an experiment to test the claim.

body.html: If 𝑎= 0 at the top, then 𝑣 would remain 0 and the ball would hover. Instead it falls, so its velocity changes through the top, so the acceleration is nonzero. Work (experiment): Toss a ball straight up above a motion sensor (or film it with a scale and a high frame rate). Plot velocity against time. If gravity stopped acting at the top, the graph would show a flat piece at 𝑣= 0. The data show a smooth straight line crossing zero with a slope of about −9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> and no flat piece. Equivalently, measure the velocity just before and just after the peak: 𝛥𝑣/ 𝛥𝑡≈−9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

answer.html: No, the claim is wrong: the ball is accelerating at the top (9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> downward). Experiment: record the ball's velocity versus time with a motion sensor or video analysis; the 𝑣-𝑡 line passes through zero with constant slope −9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>, with no flat section.

check.html: If the acceleration were zero there, the ball would hover; objects never do.

items.title: Lesson 3, Revisit the Encounter the Phenomenon Question

question.html: A roller-coaster designer asks: why do sudden changes in speed or direction affect riders? What information from this lesson can help you answer the Unit and Module questions?

answer.html: Free-fall acceleration (9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> downward) shows that velocity changes steadily whenever a force such as gravity acts, and that the sign and size of 𝑎 depend on direction; combined with 𝛥𝑣= 𝑎𝛥𝑡 it shows that quick velocity changes mean large accelerations, which is what a rider feels in a sudden drop or turn. (A drop-tower rider in free fall for 3.1 s reaches 30 m/s, an acceleration of 1𝑔; a coaster that does the same in less time would have a larger one.)
